1. The animation shows inflation and whether an income annuity's payments keep up with it. "Keeping up" is defined on screen as "buys at least the first check." It uses an illustrative retiree named Ruth, with US consumer prices (CPI-U) as the yardstick. A footer says it is US-only and "history, not a forecast."

2. A flat line marks the purchasing power of the first check. A shaded band appears along it, then Ruth's line is drawn against it. Ruth's line hovers close to the first-check level for a long stretch, with small dips in yellow. At the right-hand end it drops below the line. In the last two frames the chart gives way to a row of small white boxes, a figure of Ruth, and a refrigerator. The boxes appear to stand for what each year's check buys. They are mostly white, and the last one is dark.

3. The most natural reading is that a fixed payment buys less as prices rise. Ruth's check roughly keeps pace for a while, but late in the period it falls below what the first check bought. The dark box at the end seems to mark the point where a check no longer covers what it used to. The "ILLUSTRATIVE" labels mean this is an example, not real data for a specific person or product.

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer might infer that purchasing power matters as well as the dollar amount. They might also infer that a payout that doesn't adjust for inflation could lose ground over a long retirement. But the frames don't recommend either option.

5. The advice in 4 is my own inference. The animation only defines "keeping up" and shows the shortfall, and it says outright that it is history and not a forecast.
